| [NOTE-015](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-015.md) v2 | Periodic vehicle routing and facility location for waste collection | The paper couples bin-capacity choice with weekly periodic capacitated routing (Sunday off, cyclic). Service time depends on the chosen bin combination, which gives an MIQP; a Glover linearisation turns it into a MILP. It solves both with Gurobi 10 for 8 h, and also with a binary-mask + permutation GA (CX 0.8, EM 0.05, pop 100, 10,000 generations). On five 12-point instances Gurobi stops at 26–32% optimality gaps. The best-of-30 GA overall cost is on average −0.08% vs the MILP incumbent and +1.70% vs the MIQP incumbent; the GA mean or median is +3.75% and +5.61%. The GA routes better (−5.75% and −5.74% routing cost) but buys much more bin capacity (+19.88% and +22.59%). On 40–163-point Bahía Blanca instances the GA returns feasible solutions in 0.72–5.58 h per run, with no bound to compare against. | Read |
| [NOTE-062](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-062.md) v2 | Başar, Meyn & Perkins, control system theory notes | A conventional first-year graduate course in linear state-space control. Its most useful non-standard content is the Pendubot thread (Chs 1, 9, 10): an observer-based design from one sensor is fragile (the compensator has an unstable pole at s ≈ 46.4), while full-state LQR has \|S(jω)\| ≤ 1, infinite gain margin and ±60° phase margin. | [NOTE-889](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-889.md) | Gupta — Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse | Gupta states view selection on general AND-OR view graphs as minimizing frequency-weighted query cost plus update-frequency-weighted maintenance cost under a space budget. He proves greedy guarantees of 1 − 1/e (about 63%) of the optimal benefit, with the budget overrun by one view or up to double, but almost all of them assume no updates. Maintenance cost enters exactly one theorem: AND view graphs (each view has one way of being computed) in which every view is queried more often than it is updated. For OR view graphs, which include Harinarayan, Rajaraman and Ullman's data cube, the paper sets update costs aside outright, so it does not add upkeep to that problem. Maintenance is an abstract per-update charge for keeping a view consistent. Nothing prices building a view, tolerated staleness or deferred refresh, and there are no experiments. | Read |
| [NOTE-890](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-890.md) | Gupta & Mumick — Selection of views to materialize under a maintenance cost constraint | Gupta and Mumick choose views to materialize so as to minimize frequency-weighted query cost subject to a cap S on total maintenance time, the sum over chosen views of update frequency times a per-update maintenance cost that depends on which other views are stored. Because storing one view can make another cheaper to maintain, benefit per unit of maintenance is not monotone and the single-view greedy of earlier work can be arbitrarily bad. For OR view graphs (each view computed from one other, as in data cubes) a greedy that adds whole "inverted tree sets" gets at least 1 − 1/e (63%) of the benefit of an optimal solution that may use as much maintenance as the greedy did, the greedy using up to 2S, assuming no inverted-tree piece of the optimum alone exceeds S (Theorem 1, unproved here); without that assumption it gets half the optimum's benefit per unit of maintenance (Theorem 2). Each greedy stage enumerates exponentially many sets in general; for general AND-OR graphs there is only an exact A* search with exponential worst case. Upkeep is a budget, not a term traded against query savings; build cost, storage and staleness are not modelled, and the experiments are on random graphs of 10 to 25 nodes. | Read |
| [NOTE-895](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-895.md) | Harinarayan, Rajaraman & Ullman — Implementing data cubes efficiently | Treats a data cube's group-by queries as a lattice in which a query can be answered from any stored ancestor, prices a query at the number of rows of the smallest materialized ancestor, and chooses which views to precompute. Choosing k views to maximize the total reduction in query cost (the "benefit") is NP-complete; a greedy rule that adds the view of largest marginal benefit gets at least 1 − ((k−1)/k)^k ≥ (e−1)/e ≈ 63% of the optimal benefit, a bound that is tight, holds unchanged with query-frequency weights, and weakens to 0.63 − f under a space budget when no view takes more than a fraction f of it. The cost of building views is represented only by their size, maintenance and updates are not modelled, the data are static, and the bound is on benefit, not on query cost. On TPC-D data the greedy order reaches nearly the minimum total query time with five views and barely more space than the base view. | Read |
| [NOTE-898](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-898.md) | Finkelstein, Schkolnick & Tiberio — Physical database design for relational databases | DBDSGN chooses, for each table, one clustered (ordering) index and a set of nonclustered indices to minimise a frequency-weighted sum of per-statement costs (access, tuple update, index maintenance) plus a weighted storage term, under an optional page limit, taking every cost from the System R optimizer's own estimates rather than an external model. Statement costs for any configuration are computed exactly from "atomic" configurations with at most one index per table (Propositions 1 and 2), so the optimizer is consulted a linear rather than exponential number of times per table; with no elimination heuristics and a full search the tool finds the optimum, but only with respect to the optimizer's estimates. The paper gives one worked example and no measurement of actual execution, and its claims that the heuristics usually find the best solutions are not backed by reported data. The model is steady-state over a period: it has no term for the one-time cost of building an index or sorting a table, so it prices upkeep against retrieval, not a one-off sort against later retrievals. | Read |
| [NOTE-900](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-900.md) | Chaudhuri & Narasayya — An efficient, cost-driven index selection tool for Microsoft SQL Server | The AutoAdmin tool picks at most k indexes (single- or two-column, clustered or not) for a given workload of SQL statements, minimising the unweighted sum of the optimizer's estimated costs of those statements, with hypothetical ("what-if") indexes made visible to the optimizer by loading their statistics into the catalog. Its contribution is search efficiency: candidates are restricted to indexes in some single query's best configuration, enumeration is Greedy(m, k) (an exhaustive seed of m indexes, then greedy additions), costs of most configurations are derived from a few "atomic" ones, and two-column indexes are generated only from winning single columns. On five TPC-D workloads this cut running time to 10–24% of a baseline, with estimated-cost quality 0–7% worse, and Greedy(2, 4) matched the exhaustive optimum on four of five workloads and was within 1% on the fifth. The cost model has no build cost, no storage term and no frequency weights, the budget is a count of indexes, the workload is fixed, there is no guarantee for the greedy step, and quality is never measured by executing anything. | Read |
| [NOTE-901](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-901.md) | Gupta & Mumick — Selection of views to materialize in a data warehouse (TKDE 2005) | The journal paper merges Gupta's 1997 space-budget results and the 1999 maintenance-budget results into one article; it adds proofs, not new problems or new guarantees. | [NOTE-906](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-906.md) | Cho & Garcia-Molina — Synchronizing a database to improve freshness (SIGMOD 2000) | For a local copy of N items, each changing as an independent Poisson process with a known rate and refreshed at fixed intervals under a fixed total refresh rate, refreshing every item equally keeps the copy fresher and younger on average than refreshing in proportion to change rate, under any distribution of rates (proved in the technical report by convexity). The freshness-optimal allocation is neither: it rises and then falls with change rate, and gives no refresh at all to items that change too fast for the budget, while the age-optimal allocation rises slowly with change rate. On estimates from 270 web sites, proportional, uniform and optimal refresh give freshness 0.12, 0.57 and 0.62. Every item matters equally, staleness is a time average with no access or query model, the refresh budget is fixed rather than priced, and refresh, change and its detection are free of any other cost. | Read |
| [NOTE-908](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-908.md) | Labrinidis & Roussopoulos — WebView materialization | For a page built from database queries, the paper compares three ways to serve it on a server with online updates: compute it on each request (virt), store the query result in the DBMS and refresh it on every update (matdb), or store the finished page as a file at the web server and rewrite it on every update (matweb). It gives a cost model summing access and update costs by their frequencies and states the selection problem (choose a policy per page to minimize mean response time, no space limit, no staleness allowed), but gives no algorithm for it. On one Apache/Informix testbed with cheap indexed queries, matweb answered 10 to 230 times faster than the other two at all loads tried, and matdb was slower than virt whenever there were updates, because reading the stored result cost about as much as recomputing it. Staleness is defined as the delay from update to reply, sketched, and never measured; build cost and storage are outside the model. | Read |
| [NOTE-911](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-911.md) | Labrinidis & Roussopoulos — Balancing performance and data freshness in web database servers | The paper poses Online View Selection for a web server whose database takes updates while serving requests: choose, as the workload runs, which page fragments (WebViews) to keep stored and refreshed on every update and which to cache and invalidate, so as to minimize mean response time while the fraction of fresh fragments served (QoD) stays above a threshold θ. Its algorithm, OVIS(θ), estimates per fragment the response-time and QoD change of switching, and periodically switches up to MAX_CHANGE fragments greedily, spending a QoD surplus on speed or buying back a deficit; it materializes everything when it detects backlog. Nothing is proved: optimality of the greedy step is asserted, and the evidence is one synthetic simulation with fixed costs, in which OVIS kept QoD near θ, answered faster than caching alone, and recovered from overload. Upkeep and query savings share one cost, but staleness is a constraint set by the user, not a priced term, and build cost, switching cost and storage are absent. | Read |
| [NOTE-912](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-912.md) | Olston, Loo & Widom — Adaptive precision setting for cached approximate values | Olston, Loo and Widom set the width of each cached interval adaptively to minimize total refresh traffic. A narrow interval is escaped often (value-initiated refreshes, cost C_vr); a wide one is too imprecise for queries more often (query-initiated refreshes, cost C_qr). Under a model in which these probabilities go as 1/W² and W, the expected cost rate is least where ρ·P_vr = P_qr, ρ = 2C_vr/C_qr, and a rule that widens on value-initiated and narrows on query-initiated refreshes, with probabilities set by ρ, reached within 1% to 5% of the best fixed width in simulation. That the rule converges is argued, not proved. With exact copies required it matched an adaptive exact-caching algorithm, and where imprecision was allowed it beat it. Staleness is priced as refresh traffic only: there is no build cost, no cost of a wrong answer, and the interval is never wrong. | Read |
| [NOTE-922](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-922.md) | Olston & Widom — Offering a precision-performance tradeoff for aggregation queries over replicated data | Olston and Widom propose TRAPP: caches hold, for each numeric value, an interval its source guarantees to contain the current value, the source pushing a refresh whenever the value leaves it. A query carries a precision constraint R, and the system chooses which values to fetch exactly so that the answer interval is at most R wide whatever the true values, at least total refresh cost. For SUM (and AVG without a predicate) that choice is a 0/1 knapsack problem, NP-complete in general and polynomial with equal costs; COUNT and MIN have simple rules. Staleness becomes bounded imprecision, never error, and the cost of the source-side upkeep that guarantees this, and of setting the bound widths, is outside the optimization. The one experiment is 90 stock prices with random costs. | Read |
| [NOTE-928](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-928.md) | Linial, London & Rabinovich — the geometry of graphs | Every n-point metric embeds in ℓ₂ with distortion O(log n) in O(log n) dimensions (Theorem 3.2(1), attributed to Bourgain). The paper reproves the distortion bound by a randomized Bourgain-style construction into ℓ_p^{O(log² n)}, and it gets the dimension from Johnson–Lindenstrauss. Every embedding of a constant-degree expander into ℓ_p, 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, of any dimension, has distortion Ω(log n) (Proposition 4.2), so the bound is tight. The lower bound comes from Leighton and Rao's flow–cut gap, and the same embeddings give an O(log k) max-flow/min-cut gap for k commodities. | Read |
